cards.english: el or la — how does noun gender work in Spanish?
cards.grammarNote:
Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the article must agree:
**el** (masc. sing.) · **la** (fem. sing.) · **los** (masc. pl.) · **las** (fem. pl.)
Most **-o** nouns are masculine, most **-a** nouns are feminine — but learn every noun with its article.
cards.englishPhrase: The bread is here; the milk is there.
cards.phrase: El pan está aquí; la leche está allí.

table.title: Definite articles — gender and number
table.hint: most -o words masculine, most -a words feminine
table.note: Learn every noun with its article — el/la/los/las must match.

cards.english: He is tired / She is tired — how does the adjective change?
cards.grammarNote:
Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun or pronoun they describe:
**-o** = masculine · **-a** = feminine · add **-s** for plural.
**él está cansado** · **ella está cansada** · **ellos están cansados** · **ellas están cansadas**

cards.phrase: Él está cansado; ella está cansada.

cards.english: SER or ESTAR — identity/permanent vs state/location?
cards.grammarNote:
**ser** and **estar** both mean 'to be' but are NOT interchangeable:
**ser** → identity, origin, profession, permanent traits.
**estar** → states (emotions, health), location, temporary conditions.
*Ella es estudiante* (identity) vs *Ella está en la escuela* (location).

cards.phrase: Ella es estudiante; ella está en la escuela.

cards.english: There is / there are — hay vs está: what's the difference?
cards.grammarNote:
**hay** introduces something (indefinite — it exists): **hay un banco cerca** (there's a bank nearby).
**estar** locates something already known (definite): **el banco está en la esquina** (the bank is on the corner).
Rule of thumb: **hay** + un/una/números; **está/están** + el/la/los/las.

cards.phrase: Hay un café aquí; el café está en la esquina.

b.gloss: the known café is located here → estar

cards.english: I am hungry. (lit. 'I have hunger') — which verb do these use?
cards.grammarNote:
Spanish 'has' physical states where English 'is' them — use **tener**, not ser/estar:
**tengo hambre** (I'm hungry) · **tengo sed** (I'm thirsty) · **tengo frío** (I'm cold) · **tengo calor** (I'm hot) · **tengo miedo** (I'm afraid).

table.hint: Spanish 'has' the state; English 'is' it

cards.english: What are the present-tense forms of hablar?
cards.grammarNote:
To conjugate a regular **-AR** verb in the present tense, drop the **-ar** ending and add the personal ending.

**hablar → habl-** + ending:

**-o** (yo), **-as** (tú), **-a** (él/ella), **-amos** (nosotros), **-an** (ellos/ellas)

cards.english: What are the present-tense forms of comer and vivir?
cards.grammarNote:
-ER and -IR verbs share **four** of their five present-tense endings.

The **only** difference is nosotros: **-emos** for -ER (comemos), **-imos** for -IR (vivimos).

**comer → com-** + ending: -o, -es, -e, **-emos**, -en
**vivir → viv-** + ending: -o, -es, -e, **-imos**, -en

table.hint: they share four endings — only nosotros differs
table.note: Left = comer (-ER), right = vivir (-IR). Only the nosotros ending is different.

cards.english: What is the irregular yo form of tener, hacer, salir, ver, dar, and saber?
cards.word: tengo, hago, salgo, veo, doy, sé
cards.grammarNote:
Some verbs are **regular in every person except yo**. The yo form is irregular; all other forms follow normal -ar/-er/-ir endings.

**tengo** (tener), **hago** (hacer), **salgo** (salir), **veo** (ver), **doy** (dar), **sé** (saber)
cards.englishPhrase: I have a coffee.

table.title: Irregular yo forms (regular everywhere else)
table.hint: all other persons follow regular endings
table.note: All other persons (tú, él, nosotros…) are regular for these verbs.

cards.english: What are the present-tense forms of ir and venir?
cards.grammarNote:
**ir** (to go) uses the stem *v-* — it is completely irregular in the present.

**ir**: voy, vas, va, vamos, van

**venir** (to come) has an irregular yo (**vengo**) and e→ie stem changes elsewhere.

**venir**: vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, vienen
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the café; she comes from the office.
cards.phrase: Yo voy al café; ella viene de la oficina.

table.title: IR · VENIR — present tense
table.hint: ir is fully irregular; venir has irregular yo (vengo) and e→ie elsewhere
table.note: Columns: ir · venir. nosotros vamos / venimos keep the original stem.

cards.english: SER vs ESTAR — when to use each
cards.grammarNote:
Both **ser** and **estar** mean *to be* but are not interchangeable.

**ser** → identity, permanent traits (who/what something fundamentally is).
**estar** → states, locations, conditions (how something is right now).

*Ella es estudiante* (identity) vs *Ella está en la escuela* (location).

cards.english: What are the present-tense forms of querer (e→ie stem-changer)?
cards.grammarNote:
**querer** and **pensar** are e→ie stem-changers.

The stem vowel **e** becomes **ie** in all forms **except nosotros**, which keeps the original stem.

**querer**: quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, quieren
**pensar**: pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, piensan
cards.englishPhrase: I want a coffee.

table.title: querer (e→ie) — present tense
table.hint: e→ie everywhere except nosotros — the boot shape
table.note: nosotros keeps the original stem (no change). pensar follows the same pattern: pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, piensan.

cards.english: What are the present-tense forms of poder (o→ue stem-changer)?
cards.grammarNote:
**poder** is an o→ue stem-changer.

The stem vowel **o** becomes **ue** in all forms **except nosotros**.

**poder**: puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden
**encontrar**: encuentro, encuentras, encuentra, encontramos, encuentran

Special: **jugar** changes **u→ue** (juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, juegan).
cards.englishPhrase: I can speak Spanish.

table.title: poder (o→ue) — present tense
table.hint: o→ue everywhere except nosotros — the boot shape
table.note: nosotros keeps the original stem. encontrar → encuentro follows the same pattern. jugar is special: u→ue (juego).

cards.english: What are the preterite forms of hablar?
cards.grammarNote:
The **preterite** describes a single, completed past action. For regular **-ar** verbs, drop **-ar** and add: **-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron**.

**hablar → habl-** + ending:

Accents only on **yo** (-é) and **él/ella** (-ó).
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I spoke Spanish.

table.title: hablar (to speak) — preterite
table.hint: regular -AR verb: drop -ar, add the preterite ending
table.note: Accents on hablé and habló only. trabajar, estudiar, cocinar, llegar, caminar follow the same pattern.

cards.english: What are the preterite forms of comer and vivir?
cards.grammarNote:
-er and -ir verbs share the **same** preterite endings: **-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron**.

**comer → com-** + ending: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron
**vivir → viv-** + ending: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron

Every form has an accent except **-iste** and **-imos**.

table.title: comer (-ER) · vivir (-IR) — preterite
table.hint: -er and -ir share identical preterite endings
table.note: -er and -ir are identical in the preterite. beber → bebí follows the same pattern.

cards.english: What are the irregular preterite forms of ser/ir, estar, tener, hacer?
cards.grammarNote:
These common verbs have irregular preterite stems and use the endings **-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron** (no accent on yo or él).

**ser / ir** share the same preterite — context decides the meaning.

**hacer**: yo hice but él **hizo** (z spelling change).
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I went to the café and had coffee.
cards.phrase: Ayer fui al café y tuve un café.

table.title: Common irregular preterites
table.hint: new stem + -e/-iste/-o/-imos/-ieron, no accents
table.note: ser and ir are identical in the preterite — context tells them apart. No written accents on any of these forms.

Last night I was at the office.

cards.english: What are the imperfect forms of hablar?
cards.grammarNote:
The **imperfect** describes past habits, repeated actions, or background states — 'used to' or 'was ‑ing'. For regular **-ar** verbs: **-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -aban**.

Note: yo and él/ella are **identical** (hablaba). Only nosotros carries an accent (hablábamos).
cards.englishPhrase: I used to speak Spanish at school.

table.title: hablar (to speak) — imperfect
table.hint: regular -AR: -aba / -abas / -aba / -ábamos / -aban
table.note: yo and él/ella are identical (hablaba). trabajar, estudiar, cocinar, caminar follow the same pattern.

cards.english: What are the imperfect forms of comer, vivir — and the 3 irregular imperfects?
cards.grammarNote:
-er and -ir verbs share imperfect endings **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían** — every form has an accent on the **í**.

The imperfect has only **three** irregular verbs:
**ser → era**, **ir → iba**, **ver → veía**. Everything else is regular.
cards.englishPhrase: I used to eat at the café; I used to go there every day.
cards.phrase: Comía en el café; iba allí siempre.

table.title: Imperfect: -ER/-IR + the 3 irregulars
table.hint: -ía on every form; accent always on the i
table.note: Only 3 irregular imperfects: ser → era / eras / era; ir → iba / ibas / iba; ver → veía / veías / veía.

cards.englishPhrase: I used to speak Spanish at the café.
She used to eat at home every day.

cards.english: Preterite vs imperfect — one event or a habit?
cards.grammarNote:
Both preterite and imperfect describe the past, but they frame it differently.

**Preterite** = one finished event, a chain of events, or a specific point in time.
**Imperfect** = a habit, a repeated action, or background/ongoing description.

Time clues: *ayer, anoche, la semana pasada* → preterite. *siempre, nunca, de niño* → imperfect.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I ate at the restaurant; I used to eat at home.
cards.phrase: Ayer comí en el restaurante; comía en casa.

contrast.prompt: One finished event or a recurring habit?

cards.englishPhrase: She was always happy at school.
cards.phrase: Ella siempre era feliz en la escuela.

cards.english: What are the simple future forms of hablar?
cards.grammarNote:
The **simple future** adds one set of endings to the **whole infinitive** — the same for -ar, -er, and -ir verbs.

**hablar → hablar-** + ending:

**-é** (yo), **-ás** (tú), **-á** (él/ella), **-emos** (nosotros), **-án** (ellos/ellas)

Accent marks appear on every form except nosotros.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will speak Spanish.

table.title: hablar (to speak) — simple future
table.hint: add endings to the full infinitive — same for -ar/-er/-ir
table.note: nosotros is the only form without an accent. Same endings for comer→comeré, vivir→viviré.

cards.english: What are the conditional forms of hablar?
cards.grammarNote:
The **conditional** ('would') also attaches to the **whole infinitive** — the same for all verb types.

**hablar → hablar-** + ending:

**-ía** (yo), **-ías** (tú), **-ía** (él/ella), **-íamos** (nosotros), **-ían** (ellos/ellas)

Every form carries an accent on the **í**. yo and él/ella share the same form (-ía).
cards.englishPhrase: I would speak Spanish at home.

table.title: hablar (to speak) — conditional
table.hint: add -ía endings to the full infinitive — accent on every í
table.note: yo and él/ella are identical (-ía). Same endings for comer→comería, vivir→viviría.

cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will speak Spanish at the restaurant.
cards.phrase: Mañana hablaré español en el restaurante.

cards.englishPhrase: I would eat at the café a lot.
We will live near the school.

cards.phrase: Ellos hablarían más español en la oficina.

cards.english: What are the irregular future/conditional stems of tener, poder, hacer, salir, and decir?
cards.grammarNote:
Some verbs use an **irregular stem** in both the future and the conditional, but take the **normal endings**.

Future endings: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án
Conditional endings: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían

The stem is shared — learn it once for both tenses.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will have to work; I would do it now.
cards.phrase: Mañana tendré que trabajar; lo haría ahora.

table.title: Irregular future/conditional stems (shared)
table.hint: same stem for future (-é) and conditional (-ía)
table.note: Irregular stem + normal endings. querer→querr-, venir→vendr-, saber→sabr- follow the same pattern.

cards.grammarNote:
Future and conditional share the **same stem** (regular or irregular); only the endings differ.

**Future** (-é / -ás…) = 'will' → a plan or prediction.
**Conditional** (-ía / -ías…) = 'would' → hypothetical, wish, or polite request.

Key contrast: *hablaré* (I will speak) vs. *hablaría* (I would speak).

cards.english: I want a coffee vs. I would like a coffee — direct or polite?
cards.grammarNote:
The **conditional** softens requests to sound polite.

**quiero** (I want) → direct.
**me gustaría** (I would like) → polite conditional of *gustar*.
**¿podría...?** (could you...?) → polite conditional of *poder*.

Use the conditional when making polite requests or asking for things in formal situations.

cards.phrase: Quiero un café → Me gustaría un café, por favor.

cards.englishPhrase: I would like a coffee, please.

cards.english: What are the direct object pronouns in Spanish?
cards.grammarNote:
A **direct object** receives the action of the verb. Replace it with a **direct object pronoun** placed **before the conjugated verb**.

**me** = me | **te** = you | **lo/la** = him/her/it | **nos** = us | **los/las** = them

lo/la and los/las must match the **gender and number** of the noun replaced.
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee? I want it.

table.title: Direct object pronouns
table.hint: placed before the conjugated verb; lo/la agree with the noun's gender
table.note: lo/la and los/las must match the gender and number of the noun they replace.

cards.english: Which direct object pronoun replaces 'el café' (masc.) vs 'la comida' (fem.)?
cards.grammarNote:
The third-person direct object pronoun must agree in **gender and number** with the noun it replaces.

**lo** = masculine singular (el café, el pan…)
**la** = feminine singular (la comida, la leche…)
**los** = masculine plural (los platos…)
**las** = feminine plural (las manzanas…)

cards.phrase: Quiero el café. → Lo quiero. / Necesito la comida. → La necesito.

produce.gloss: lo → masc. sg. | la → fem. sg. | los → masc. pl.

cards.english: Pronoun placement: before conjugated verb OR attached to infinitive — both correct?
cards.grammarNote:
With **conjugated verb + infinitive**, the direct object pronoun has two equally correct positions:
1. **Before the conjugated verb**: *Lo quiero comer.*
2. **Attached to the infinitive**: *Quiero comerlo.*

Both sentences mean exactly the same thing.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to eat it.

contrast.prompt: Both are correct — where does 'lo' go?

cards.english: What are the indirect object pronouns in Spanish (to/for whom)?
cards.grammarNote:
The **indirect object pronoun** marks the recipient — 'to/for whom'. It goes **before the conjugated verb**.

**me** = to me | **te** = to you | **le** = to him/her/usted | **nos** = to us | **les** = to them

With **dar**, **decir**, **servir**: *le doy el café* (I give the coffee to him/her).
cards.englishPhrase: I give the menu to her.

table.title: Indirect object pronouns
table.hint: marks the recipient (to/for whom); goes before the conjugated verb
table.note: le and les do NOT change for gender — they are the same for masculine and feminine.

cards.english: lo (direct) vs. le (indirect): sees him vs. gives to him
cards.word: lo veo / le doy el café
cards.grammarNote:
**lo** = direct object — the person/thing directly acted on (who/what is seen, bought, found…).
**le** = indirect object — the recipient ('to/for whom').

When you **give** something **to** someone, the 'something' is direct (lo/la) and the 'someone' is indirect (le).
cards.englishPhrase: I see him; I give him the coffee.
cards.phrase: Lo veo; le doy el café.

contrast.prompt: Which pronoun: sees him (direct) or gives to him (indirect)?

b.gloss: I give him the coffee → indirect / recipient (le)

cards.english: le/les + lo/la → se lo / se la (never 'le lo')
cards.grammarNote:
When **le** or **les** appears **before lo / la / los / las**, the **le/les becomes se**. *Le lo* is never allowed — it always changes to **se lo**.

*¿El menú? Le lo doy.* ✗ → *¿El menú? **Se lo** doy a María.* ✓

The order is still indirect first, then direct.
cards.englishPhrase: The menu? I give it to her.
cards.phrase: ¿El menú? Se lo doy a María.

cloze.prompt: to her (María) + it — le → ? before lo

cards.english: Double object pronouns: indirect always comes first, then direct
cards.word: me lo / te la / se lo
cards.grammarNote:
When a sentence has **two object pronouns**, the **indirect pronoun comes first**, then the direct: **indirect + direct**.

*Me lo da.* (He gives it to me.) — me = indirect, lo = direct.

If the indirect is le/les and direct is lo/la, remember: **le → se**.
cards.englishPhrase: He gives it (the coffee) to me.

table.title: Two pronouns: indirect first, then direct
table.hint: le/les → se before lo/la/los/las
rows: me lo da (gives it to me)
te la doy (I give it to you)
se lo doy (I give it to him/her)
table.note: Order is always: indirect first, then direct. le + lo never stays as 'le lo' — always se lo.

cards.english: por vs para — which one points forward to a goal, and which one looks back at a cause?
cards.grammarNote:
**PARA** points **forward** — goal, destination, recipient, deadline. The finish line ahead.

**POR** looks **backward or through** — cause, exchange, duration, route. The motive behind or the path through.

Memory hook: PARA = *purpose ahead*; POR = *reason behind / path through*.

cards.phrase: La comida es para ti. / Gracias por la comida.

b.gloss: backward / through — cause / exchange / duration / route

cards.english: What are the four core uses of para?
cards.grammarNote:
**para** points forward to a **goal, recipient, deadline, or destination** — the finish line ahead.

Wherever PARA appears, something is aimed *at* a target.
cards.englishPhrase: I study in order to learn Spanish.

table.title: Uses of PARA
table.hint: para points forward — to a goal, a person, a deadline, a place
table.note: All four uses share one idea: PARA aims at a target ahead.

cards.english: What are the four core uses of por?
cards.grammarNote:
**por** looks back at the **cause or reason**, covers **exchange and gratitude**, marks **duration or time of day**, and shows **movement through** a place.

Think: *the motive / the route / the span.*
cards.englishPhrase: Thanks for the food.

table.title: Uses of POR
table.hint: por looks back or through — at the cause, the span, the route
table.note: All four uses share one idea: por points to the motive, the route, or the span — never the goal.

cards.english: por el parque vs para el parque — passing through or heading toward?
cards.grammarNote:
Same place, opposite meanings:

**por** = movement *through* or *along* (the place is the route).
**para** = movement *toward* (the place is the destination).

*Camino por el parque* → through the park.
*Salgo para el parque* → headed for the park.
cards.englishPhrase: I walk through the park. / I leave for the park.
cards.phrase: Camino por el parque. / Salgo para el parque.

contrast.prompt: Same place — passing through it or heading toward it?

b.gloss: para = destination — the park is where you are headed

cards.english: What fixed everyday expressions are built with por?
cards.word: por favor · ¿por qué? · por la mañana · por la noche
cards.grammarNote:
Several everyday phrases you already use are built with **por**.

They all fit the same pattern: **por** points to a reason, a span, or an exchange — even inside fixed expressions.
cards.englishPhrase: Please — why do you work at night?
cards.phrase: Por favor, ¿por qué trabajas por la noche?

table.title: Fixed POR expressions
table.hint: all use por — cause, span, or exchange
table.note: Every phrase uses por because it points to a cause, a span, or an exchange — the same core idea.

cards.english: es para (recipient) vs gracias por (exchange) — which is which?
cards.grammarNote:
Both translate as *for* in English but are NOT interchangeable:

**Es para ti** → the item is *intended for* you (recipient — para points forward to the person).
**Gracias por el café** → thanks *in return for* the coffee (exchange — por looks back at what was received).
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee is for you. / Thanks for the coffee.
cards.phrase: El café es para ti. / Gracias por el café.

a.gloss: para = recipient — the coffee is intended for you

b.gloss: por = exchange — thanks in return for the coffee

cards.englishPhrase: I leave for the office.
I walk through the park.
The food is for you.
Please, can you help me?
Why are you tired?

cards.english: How do you form a regular affirmative tú command?
cards.grammarNote:
For an affirmative **tú** command, use the **él/ella** present-tense form — drop the infinitive and add the regular 3rd-person ending.

**hablar → habla** (speak!), **comer → come** (eat!), **escribir → escribe** (write!)

This works for all regular -ar, -er, and -ir verbs.
cards.englishPhrase: Speak with the waiter.

table.title: Affirmative tú commands — regular verbs
table.hint: same as the él/ella present form
table.note: Works for ALL regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs. Pattern: drop -ar/-er/-ir and add the él/ella ending.

cards.english: How do you form a negative tú command?
cards.grammarNote:
For a **negative tú** command, take the **yo** present form, drop **-o**, and add the *opposite* vowel ending:

**-ar** verbs: add **-es** → no hables, no compres
**-er / -ir** verbs: add **-as** → no comas, no escribas

This is the present subjunctive — the vowel flips.
cards.englishPhrase: Don't eat the cake.

table.title: Negative tú commands
table.hint: yo form − o + opposite vowel ending
table.note: -ar verbs take -es; -er and -ir verbs take -as. The vowel is the opposite of the affirmative.

cards.english: Eat! vs Don't eat! — what changes?
cards.grammarNote:
Affirmative and negative **tú** commands use completely different forms:
**come** = él/ella present tense (affirmative)
**no comas** = subjunctive (negative — vowel flips)

The negative is NOT just adding *no* to the affirmative.
cards.englishPhrase: Eat the salad, don't eat the cake.
cards.phrase: Come la ensalada; no comas el pastel.

cards.englishPhrase: Speak with the waiter, please.
cards.phrase: Habla con el camarero, por favor.

cards.englishPhrase: Don't eat that; it's bad.
Wait here at the café.
Don't buy food at the store now.
cards.phrase: No compres comida en la tienda ahora.

cards.english: What are the irregular affirmative tú commands?
cards.word: di, haz, ve, ven, sal, ten
cards.grammarNote:
Eight verbs have short irregular **tú** commands — memorise them:

**decir → di** (say!), **hacer → haz** (do/make!), **ir → ve** (go!), **venir → ven** (come!), **salir → sal** (leave!), **tener → ten** (have/hold!)

These irregulars apply ONLY to the affirmative tú command.
cards.englishPhrase: Come here and have some coffee.
cards.phrase: Ven aquí y ten un café.

table.title: Irregular affirmative tú commands
table.hint: six key verbs — memorise the short forms
table.note: These short forms apply ONLY to the affirmative tú command. Negative commands use the regular subjunctive: no digas, no hagas, no vayas…

cards.english: How do you form a formal usted command?
cards.grammarNote:
For a polite **usted** command, use the subjunctive (yo stem + opposite vowel):

**-ar → -e**: hablar → yo hablo → **hable**
**-er/-ir → -a**: comer → yo como → **coma**

Same form for affirmative and negative — just add **no** for negative: **no hable**.
cards.englishPhrase: Speak with the customer, please.
cards.phrase: Hable con el cliente, por favor.

table.title: Formal usted commands
table.hint: yo form − o + opposite vowel
table.note: -ar → -e, -er/-ir → -a. For negative, add no: no hable, no coma. Irregular yo forms carry over: salgo → salga.

cards.english: Where do pronouns go in affirmative commands?
cards.grammarNote:
In **affirmative** commands, object and reflexive pronouns **attach to the end** of the verb. An accent mark is added to keep the original stress:

**ayuda + me → ayúdame** (help me)
**haz + lo → hazlo** (do it)
**di + me + lo → dímelo** (tell me it)

In **negative** commands, pronouns go **before** the verb: **no me ayudes**, **no lo hagas**.
cards.englishPhrase: Help me, please.

table.title: Pronoun placement — affirmative vs negative
table.hint: affirmative: attach to end; negative: before the verb
table.note: Affirmative: pronouns attach (accent preserves stress). Negative: pronouns stay before the conjugated verb.

cards.english: Do it / Make it (irregular tú command)
cards.englishPhrase: Do it now, please.
Come to the restaurant with us.
Tell me where the café is.
Speak with the customer, please.
cards.phrase: Hable con el cliente, por favor.

cards.englishPhrase: Leave the restaurant now.

cards.english: Don't do it (negative command + pronoun before verb)
cards.englishPhrase: Don't do it at school.
cards.phrase: No lo hagas en la escuela.

cards.english: What are the present-tense forms of haber (the helper for 'have done')?
cards.grammarNote:
The present perfect = **haber** (present) + past participle.

Learn the helper: **he, has, ha, hemos, han**.

Do not confuse with **tener** — 'to have' for possession. Haber is used only for perfect tenses.
cards.englishPhrase: I have eaten at the restaurant.

table.title: haber — present tense (helper verb)
table.hint: use this form + participle for 'have done'
table.note: haber is only a helper here — 'to have/own' is tener.

cards.english: How do you form regular past participles (-ado / -ido)?
cards.grammarNote:
Drop the infinitive ending and add:

**-ar → -ado** (hablar → hablado)

**-er → -ido** (comer → comido)

**-ir → -ido** (vivir → vivido)

The participle never changes for gender or number after haber.
cards.englishPhrase: We have worked a lot today.

table.title: Regular past participles
table.hint: -ar → -ado; -er / -ir → -ido
table.note: After haber, the participle always ends in -o — never -a or -os.

cards.english: How do you say 'I have spoken' and 'she has eaten' (present perfect)?
cards.grammarNote:
Join haber (present) + participle:

**yo → he hablado** (I have spoken)

**ella → ha comido** (she has eaten)

The participle stays fixed — only haber changes.
cards.englishPhrase: I have spoken a little Spanish.
cards.phrase: He hablado un poco de español.

produce.task: Say 'we have eaten' and 'they have worked'

cards.english: Pick the right form of haber: 'she has eaten'
cards.grammarNote:
Only **haber** changes with the subject; the participle stays fixed:

**yo he comido**, **ella ha comido**, **ellos han comido**.
cards.englishPhrase: She has eaten at the restaurant.
cards.phrase: Ella ha comido en el restaurante.

cloze.prompt: she has eaten (él/ella form of haber)

cards.englishPhrase: I have eaten at the café.
We have spoken Spanish today.
She has lived near the school.
cards.phrase: Ella ha vivido cerca de la escuela.

cards.englishPhrase: They have worked a lot.

cards.english: What are the irregular past participles for hacer, decir, ver, volver, escribir, and freír?
cards.word: hecho, dicho, visto, vuelto, escrito, frito
cards.grammarNote:
These common verbs do **not** follow -ado/-ido — memorise them:

**hacer → hecho**, **decir → dicho**, **ver → visto**

**volver → vuelto**, **escribir → escrito**, **freír → frito**
cards.englishPhrase: I have made the food.

table.title: Irregular past participles
table.hint: these don't follow -ado/-ido — learn as fixed forms
table.note: Never say 'hacido', 'decido', or 'volvido' — only hecho, dicho, vuelto.

cards.english: Pick the correct participle of hacer: 'what have you done?'
cards.grammarNote:
**hacer → hecho**, never 'hacido'.

**¿Qué has hecho?** = What have you done?
cards.englishPhrase: What have you done today?

cloze.prompt: what have you done? (participle of hacer)

cards.english: How do you form the past perfect ('had done') with haber?
cards.grammarNote:
The past perfect ('had done') = **haber in the imperfect** + participle:

**había comido** (I had eaten)

The same participles are used — only the helper changes from present to imperfect.
cards.englishPhrase: I had already eaten.

table.title: haber — imperfect (for past perfect / pluperfect)
table.hint: same participles as present perfect — only the helper changes
table.note: había comido = had eaten; hemos comido = have eaten. Helper tense makes the difference.

cards.english: What is the difference between 'he comido' and 'había comido'?
cards.grammarNote:
Choose the helper's tense:

**he comido** = I have eaten (result connects to now)

**había comido** = I had eaten (before another past moment)
cards.englishPhrase: I had eaten before you arrived.
cards.phrase: Había comido antes de que llegaras.

a.gloss: have eaten — result connects to now

b.gloss: had eaten — before another past event

cards.englishPhrase: I have made the food.
He has seen the restaurant.
I had eaten at home.
We had spoken Spanish before.

cards.english: What is the 'opposite vowel' rule for forming the present subjunctive?
cards.grammarNote:
Start from the **yo** form of the present tense, drop the **-o**, and add the *opposite* vowel endings:

**-ar** verbs use **-e** endings (like -er verbs normally do).
**-er / -ir** verbs use **-a** endings (like -ar verbs normally do).

The yo form carries any stem irregularity into all subjunctive forms.
cards.englishPhrase: I want you to speak Spanish.

table.title: The 'opposite vowel' rule
table.hint: yo form → drop -o → add opposite vowel endings
table.note: -ar verbs take -e endings; -er/-ir verbs take -a endings.

cards.english: What are all the present-subjunctive forms of hablar?
cards.grammarNote:
For regular **-ar** verbs, drop -o from the yo form (hablo → habl-) and add: **-e, -es, -e, -emos, -en**.

The same endings apply to all regular -ar verbs: trabajar, cocinar, estudiar, ayudar, caminar, viajar.
cards.englishPhrase: I hope you work at the office.
cards.phrase: Espero que trabajes en la oficina.

table.title: hablar — present subjunctive
table.hint: regular -ar verb: drop -o, add -e endings
table.note: Same pattern for trabajar → trabaje, estudiar → estudie, cocinar → cocine.

cards.english: What are all the present-subjunctive forms of comer and vivir?
cards.grammarNote:
For **-er / -ir** verbs, drop -o from the yo form and add: **-a, -as, -a, -amos, -an**.

**comer → coma, comas, coma, comamos, coman**
**vivir → viva, vivas, viva, vivamos, vivan**

Both -er and -ir share the same endings in the subjunctive.
cards.englishPhrase: I want you to eat at the restaurant.
cards.phrase: Quiero que comas en el restaurante.

table.title: comer · vivir — present subjunctive
table.hint: -er and -ir share the same -a endings
table.note: Left = comer, right = vivir. Same endings for all regular -er/-ir verbs.

cards.englishPhrase: I hope you speak Spanish at school.
cards.phrase: Espero que hables español en la escuela.

cards.englishPhrase: I want you to eat at home.
I hope she works at the office.
cards.phrase: Espero que trabaje en la oficina.

cards.englishPhrase: I want us to study at the library.
cards.phrase: Quiero que estudiemos en la biblioteca.

cards.english: What are the six fully irregular subjunctive forms?
cards.word: sea, vaya, esté, dé, sepa, haya
cards.grammarNote:
Six verbs are completely irregular in the subjunctive — they don't follow the yo-form rule. Memorise them:

**ser → sea**, **ir → vaya**, **estar → esté**, **dar → dé**, **saber → sepa**, **haber → haya**

These irregular stems apply to all persons: sea, seas, sea, seamos, sean.
cards.englishPhrase: I hope she is happy.

table.title: Fully irregular subjunctives
table.hint: these don't come from the yo form
table.note: Learn as fixed forms. Example: ir → vaya, vayas, vaya, vayamos, vayan.

cards.english: When does a wish verb trigger the subjunctive?
cards.grammarNote:
Wish verbs (**querer, esperar**) take the subjunctive **only when the subject changes**:

**Same subject** → infinitive: *quiero comer* (I want to eat)
**Different subject** → que + subjunctive: *quiero que comas* (I want you to eat)

The word **que** is the bridge between the two subjects.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to eat. / I want you to eat.

cards.english: Which verbs of wishing trigger que + subjunctive?
cards.word: quiero que, espero que, necesito que
cards.grammarNote:
Verbs of wishing, wanting, and needing take **que + subjunctive** when the subject changes:

**quiero que** + subjunctive, **espero que** + subjunctive, **necesito que** + subjunctive.

The whole subjunctive clause is what the speaker wants/hopes/needs.
cards.englishPhrase: I need you to come home.

table.title: Wish triggers + que + subjunctive
table.hint: two different subjects → que + subjunctive
table.note: Wanting, hoping, or needing someone else to act → que + subjunctive.

cards.english: How do impersonal expressions (es bueno que…) work?
cards.grammarNote:
Impersonal expressions that judge an action take the subjunctive:
**es bueno que** + subjunctive, **es malo que** + subjunctive.

These phrases have no personal subject — they're value judgements about what someone else does.
cards.englishPhrase: It's good that you eat at home.
cards.phrase: Es bueno que comas en casa.

produce.task: Say 'It's good that she works' and 'It's bad that you eat there'
produce.answer: es bueno que trabaje / es malo que comas allí

cards.englishPhrase: I hope she is happy.
I want you to go to the park.
I hope he knows Spanish.
I want us to be at the café.
cards.phrase: Quiero que estemos en el café.

cards.englishPhrase: I hope they come to the restaurant.

cards.english: Which mood follows an emotional reaction + que?
cards.grammarNote:
When you express an emotional reaction to what someone else does, the verb after **que** goes into the subjunctive.

**me alegra que** (I'm glad that), **es triste que** (it's sad that), **es bueno que** (it's good that) → all trigger the subjunctive.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm glad you're here.

table.title: Emotion triggers → subjunctive
table.hint: emotional reaction + que → subjunctive
table.note: Reacting to another person's action = subjunctive. Same pattern: me gusta que, me sorprende que.

cards.english: Knowing a fact vs feeling: indicative or subjunctive after 'que'?
cards.word: sé que viene / me alegra que venga
cards.grammarNote:
The clause after **que** stays **indicative** when you are stating a known fact.
It shifts to the **subjunctive** when you are expressing an emotional reaction.

**sé que viene** (I know he's coming — factual)
**me alegra que venga** (I'm glad he's coming — emotional reaction)
cards.englishPhrase: I'm glad she's coming.

cards.english: I'm glad you're here — which form of estar?
cards.grammarNote:
After an emotion trigger + que, use the subjunctive.
**estar** → tú subjunctive = **estés**.

**me alegra que estés aquí** (I'm glad you are here).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm glad you are here.

cloze.prompt: I'm glad you are here (tú subjunctive of estar)

cards.englishPhrase: I'm glad you're here.
It's sad that you're tired.

cards.english: I like that we eat at the restaurant
cards.word: me gusta que comamos en el restaurante
cards.englishPhrase: I like that we eat at the restaurant.
cards.phrase: Me gusta que comamos en el restaurante.

cards.english: What mood follows 'no creo que' and 'tal vez'?
cards.word: no creo que venga / tal vez venga
cards.grammarNote:
Doubting or denying a claim pushes the following verb into the **subjunctive**.

**no creo que** (I don't think that), **dudo que** (I doubt that), **tal vez** (maybe) all express uncertainty → subjunctive.

Note: affirmed **creo que** takes the indicative.
cards.englishPhrase: I don't think he's coming today.

table.title: Doubt / denial → subjunctive
table.hint: uncertainty about a fact = subjunctive
table.note: Contrast: creo que viene (I think he's coming — indicative) vs no creo que venga (I don't think so — subjunctive).

cards.english: Affirmed 'I think' vs denied 'I don't think': indicative or subjunctive?
cards.word: creo que viene / no creo que venga
cards.grammarNote:
**creo que** (I think that) = belief presented as true → **indicative**.
**no creo que** (I don't think that) = doubt → **subjunctive**.

The negation flips the certainty and the mood.
cards.englishPhrase: I don't think she's coming.
I don't think he's coming.
Maybe she'll come later.

cards.english: Which conjunctions always require the subjunctive, regardless of tense?
cards.word: para que, antes de que, sin que
cards.grammarNote:
Some conjunctions introduce something not yet real or certain, so they **always** take the subjunctive — no indicative alternative exists.

**para que** (so that / in order that)
**antes de que** (before)
**sin que** (without)
cards.englishPhrase: I help you so that you learn.

table.title: Always-subjunctive conjunctions
table.hint: these always introduce something not-yet-real
table.note: Unlike cuando, these conjunctions never take the indicative — the subjunctive is mandatory.

cards.english: Same subject or different subject with 'para'?
cards.grammarNote:
When both clauses share the same subject, use **para + infinitive**.
When the subjects differ, use **para que + subjunctive**.

**trabajo para comer** (I work to eat — same subject: I)
**trabajo para que comas** (I work so you eat — different subjects: I / you)
cards.englishPhrase: I cook so that you eat.

a.gloss: same subject → infinitive (I work to eat)

b.gloss: different subject → subjunctive (I cook so you eat)

cards.english: After 'cuando', which mood: future event or habitual action?
cards.grammarNote:
**cuando** (when) triggers different moods depending on time reference:

- Future / not-yet-happened → **subjunctive**: *cuando llegue* (when I arrive — hasn't happened yet)
- Habitual / routine → **indicative**: *cuando llego* (when(ever) I arrive — routine)
cards.englishPhrase: When I arrive, I'll call you.

table.title: cuando + which mood?
table.hint: future vs routine — the mood changes
table.note: Key test: is the event certain and repeated (habit)? Use indicative. Is it pending / not yet real? Use subjunctive.

cards.englishPhrase: I explain it so that you understand.
Eat before you leave.
When I arrive, we'll eat.

cards.english: How do you form 'more … than' and 'less … than' in Spanish?
cards.grammarNote:
**más + adjective + que** = more … than (superiority).
**menos + adjective + que** = less … than (inferiority).
Put the adjective between más/menos and que:
*El café está más caliente que el té.* (The coffee is hotter than the tea.)
*La escuela es menos grande que la universidad.* (The school is less big than the university.)
cards.englishPhrase: Coffee is hotter than tea.
cards.phrase: El café está más caliente que el té.

table.title: Superiority and inferiority comparisons
table.hint: adjective goes between más/menos and que
table.note: más and menos never change form — they work with any adjective.

cards.english: How do you say 'as … as' (equality) with an adjective or a verb?
cards.grammarNote:
Equality has two patterns:
**tan + adjective + como** = as … as (with an adjective).
**tanto/a/os/as + noun + como** or **verb + tanto como** = as much/many as.
Both use **como** (not que):
*Ella está tan feliz como yo.* / *Como tanto como tú.*
cards.englishPhrase: She is as tired as me.
cards.phrase: Ella está tan cansada como yo.

table.title: Equality comparisons — tan/tanto … como
table.hint: equality always uses como, never que
table.note: tanto agrees with the noun in gender and number: tanta comida, tantos libros.

cards.englishPhrase: Coffee is hotter than tea.
cards.phrase: El café está más caliente que el té.

cards.englishPhrase: The school is less big than the university.
cards.phrase: La escuela es menos grande que la universidad.

cards.englishPhrase: He is as happy as me.
cards.phrase: Él está tan feliz como yo.

cards.englishPhrase: I eat as much as you.

cards.english: What are the four irregular comparative adjectives in Spanish?
cards.grammarNote:
Four adjectives use irregular comparatives — never add más before them:
**bueno → mejor** (better), **malo → peor** (worse), **viejo/grande → mayor** (older/greater), **joven/pequeño → menor** (younger/lesser).
They still use **que** for the comparison:
*Este café es mejor que ese.* (This coffee is better than that one.)
cards.englishPhrase: This coffee is better than that one.
cards.phrase: Este café es mejor que ese.

table.title: Irregular comparatives — never use más before these
table.hint: they still take que for the comparison
table.note: más bueno and más malo are incorrect — always say mejor and peor.

cards.english: How do you form the superlative ('the most …', 'the …-est') in Spanish?
cards.grammarNote:
Superlative = **article (el/la/los/las) + noun + más + adjective + de + group**:
*el parque más grande de la ciudad* (the biggest park in the city).
For irregulars: **el/la mejor de** (the best of), **el/la peor de** (the worst of).
The article must agree with the noun: *la escuela más tranquila del barrio.*
cards.englishPhrase: It's the biggest park in the city.
cards.phrase: Es el parque más grande de la ciudad.

table.title: Superlative — article + noun + más + adjective + de
table.hint: de links the superlative to its group
rows: el parque más grande de la ciudad
table.note: The article (el/la/los/las) must match the noun in gender and number.

cards.english: mejor vs 'más bueno' — which is correct for 'better'?
cards.grammarNote:
**mejor** is the irregular comparative of **bueno**.
Never say *más bueno* — it is incorrect.
Same rule: never say *más malo*; always say **peor**.
cards.englishPhrase: This restaurant is better.

contrast.prompt: How do you say 'better' in Spanish?

a.gloss: mejor — correct irregular comparative of bueno

cards.english: Complete the equality: 'as tired as you'
cards.grammarNote: The equality pair is **tan … como** (as … as). Both parts are fixed: tan before the adjective, como after it. Don't confuse como (equality) with que (superiority/inferiority).
cards.englishPhrase: I am as tired as you.

cards.english: Build a superlative: 'the best café in the neighborhood'
cards.grammarNote:
Superlative with irregular: **el/la mejor/peor + noun + de + group**.
For regular: **el/la + noun + más + adjective + de + group**.
cards.englishPhrase: It's the best café in the neighborhood.
cards.phrase: Es el mejor café del barrio.

produce.concept: Superlative: el/la mejor/peor + noun + de + group
produce.task: Say 'the best café in the neighborhood'

cards.englishPhrase: This coffee is better than that one.
cards.phrase: Este café es mejor que ese.

cards.englishPhrase: The food is worse today.
She is older than me.
It's the best restaurant in the city.
cards.phrase: Es el mejor restaurante de la ciudad.

cards.english: What are the Spanish reflexive pronouns (me/te/se…)?
cards.grammarNote:
A reflexive verb turns the action back on the subject ('-self'). Each subject has its own pronoun:
**me** (yo), **te** (tú), **se** (él/ella), **nos** (nosotros), **se** (ellos/ellas).

The infinitive ends in **-se** (llamarse, relajarse, quedarse).
cards.englishPhrase: My name is Ana.

table.title: Reflexive pronouns
table.hint: match the pronoun to the subject
table.note: The pronoun goes directly before the conjugated verb. Infinitives show it by ending in -se.

cards.english: What are the full conjugated forms of llamarse?
cards.word: me llamo, te llamas, se llama, nos llamamos, se llaman
cards.grammarNote:
Conjugate the verb normally, then add the matching reflexive pronoun:
**me llamo, te llamas, se llama, nos llamamos, se llaman** (literally 'I call myself…').

The verb ending changes as usual; only the pronoun shifts with the subject.
cards.englishPhrase: What is your name?

table.title: llamarse (to be called)
table.hint: pronoun + regular -AR conjugation
table.note: The verb ending follows normal -AR rules; the pronoun changes with the subject.

cards.english: How does a daily-routine reflexive verb (relajarse) conjugate?
cards.word: me relajo, te relajas, se relaja, nos relajamos, se relajan
cards.grammarNote:
All reflexive verbs follow the same pattern: pronoun + conjugated verb.

**relajarse** is regular -AR:
**me relajo, te relajas, se relaja, nos relajamos, se relajan**.

Other daily-routine reflexives follow the same template: quedarse, preocuparse, reunirse.
cards.englishPhrase: I relax at home.

table.title: relajarse (to relax) — pronoun + verb
table.hint: regular -AR endings, pronoun matches the subject
table.note: quedarse, preocuparse, and reunirse follow the same pronoun + conjugation pattern.

cards.englishPhrase: My name is Ana.
Her name is Ana.
We relax at home.
You feel tired today.

cards.english: Where can a reflexive pronoun go when there is an infinitive?
cards.grammarNote:
With a conjugated verb + infinitive, the reflexive pronoun has two equally correct positions:

1. **Attached** to the infinitive: quiero relajarme
2. **Before** the first (conjugated) verb: me quiero relajar

Both mean 'I want to relax.' Spanish speakers use both freely.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to relax at home.

table.title: Pronoun placement with infinitives
table.hint: both positions are correct — choose freely
table.note: Same rule for any reflexive + infinitive pair: quiero quedarme / me quiero quedar.

cards.english: What is the difference between dormir and dormirse?
cards.grammarNote:
Some verbs shift meaning when made reflexive:

**dormir** = to sleep (general)
**dormirse** = to fall asleep (the action happens to the subject)

Similarly: **ir** (to go) vs **irse** (to leave / go away).
cards.englishPhrase: He falls asleep at the table.
cards.phrase: Él se duerme en la mesa.

cards.english: What is the difference between preocupar and preocuparse?
cards.grammarNote:
Meaning shifts with the reflexive pronoun:

**me preocupa el trabajo** — work worries me (subject = el trabajo, action lands on me)
**me preocupo por el trabajo** — I worry about work (I am both the subject and the one who worries)
cards.englishPhrase: I worry about work.

b.gloss: I worry (reflexive — I act on myself)

cards.english: With reflexive verbs and body parts, which article do you use — las or mis?
cards.grammarNote:
When a reflexive verb involves a body part, Spanish uses the definite article (el/la/los/las), not a possessive (mi/mis).

The reflexive pronoun already shows it is yours:
**me lavo las manos** (I wash my hands) — NOT 'mis manos'.
cards.englishPhrase: I wash my hands.

cloze.prompt: I wash my hands — use the article, not the possessive

cards.english: What reflexive pronoun goes with nosotros?
cards.grammarNote:
For **nosotros**, the reflexive pronoun is **nos**:
**nos quedamos** (we stay), **nos relajamos** (we relax), **nos reunimos** (we meet).
cards.englishPhrase: We stay at the restaurant.

cloze.prompt: we stay — choose the nosotros reflexive pronoun

cards.englishPhrase: I want to relax at home.
She worries a lot.

cards.phrase: Él se queda en casa hoy.
cards.englishPhrase: He stays home today.
I worry about work.

cards.english: How do you make a sentence negative in Spanish?
cards.grammarNote:
Place **no** directly before the conjugated verb:
**no quiero** (I don't want), **no habla** (he/she doesn't speak).

Unlike English, there is no 'do / does / did' helper — just **no** before the verb.
cards.englishPhrase: She doesn't speak Spanish.

table.title: Basic negation: no + verb
table.hint: no goes directly before the conjugated verb
table.note: No helper verb ('do/does') is needed. Just place 'no' before the verb.

cards.english: What is the 'double negative' rule in Spanish?
cards.grammarNote:
Spanish **requires** a second negative word after the verb when **no** comes before it:
**no como nada** (I don't eat anything — literally 'I don't eat nothing').

Two negatives together are grammatically correct in Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: I don't want anything.

table.title: no + verb + negative word
table.hint: two negatives are required, not optional
table.note: Unlike English, Spanish demands the double negative when a negative word follows the verb.

cards.englishPhrase: She doesn't speak Spanish at school.
cards.phrase: Ella no habla español en la escuela.

cards.englishPhrase: I don't eat anything today.
Nobody comes to the restaurant today.
cards.phrase: No viene nadie al restaurante hoy.

cards.englishPhrase: I don't want anything, thank you.

cards.english: What are the affirmative and negative indefinite pairs?
cards.grammarNote:
Each positive indefinite has a negative counterpart:

**algo** (something) ↔ **nada** (nothing)
**alguien** (somebody) ↔ **nadie** (nobody)
**siempre** (always) ↔ **nunca** (never)
**también** (also) ↔ **tampoco** (neither / not either)
cards.englishPhrase: I never eat meat either.

table.title: Affirmative ↔ Negative pairs
table.hint: flip each positive to its negative counterpart
table.note: tampoco = 'not either / me neither'; use it to agree with a negative statement.

cards.english: What is the difference between 'nunca como' and 'no como nunca'?
cards.grammarNote:
**nunca** (never) has two valid positions:

1. **Before** the verb — no **no** needed: **nunca como carne**
2. **After** the verb — keep **no**: **no como carne nunca**

Both mean the same thing.
cards.englishPhrase: I never drink coffee.

table.title: Two ways to say 'never'
table.hint: before verb = no 'no'; after verb = keep 'no'
table.note: When the negative word leads the sentence, drop 'no'. When it follows the verb, keep 'no'.

cards.english: What is the opposite of 'algún / alguna' (some / any)?
cards.grammarNote:
**algún / alguna** = some / any (positive); **ningún / ninguna** = no / none (negative).

Before a masculine noun: **ningún** (shortens from ninguno).
Before a feminine noun: **ninguna**.

**¿hay algún café?** → **no, no hay ningún café**.
cards.englishPhrase: There is no café nearby.

cards.english: What is the opposite of 'también' (also / too)?
cards.grammarNote:
**también** = also / too (agrees with positives): **yo también quiero café**.
**tampoco** = neither / not either (agrees with negatives): **yo tampoco quiero nada**.
cards.englishPhrase: Me neither — I don't want coffee either.

contrast.prompt: Agreeing with a positive or a negative?

cards.englishPhrase: There is nothing in the house.
cards.phrase: No hay nada en la casa.

cards.englishPhrase: Nobody is waiting at the café.
cards.phrase: No hay nadie esperando en el café.

cards.englishPhrase: He never comes to the office.
cards.phrase: Él nunca viene a la oficina.

cards.englishPhrase: She doesn't want to eat either.
There's no restaurant here.
There's no table free.

cards.english: How do you say 'I like coffee' and 'you like coffee' with gustar?
cards.word: me gusta el café / te gusta el café
cards.grammarNote:
**gustar** literally means 'to be pleasing to'. The thing you like is the grammatical **subject**, and an indirect pronoun shows *to whom* it is pleasing.

**me gusta el café** = 'coffee is pleasing to me' = I like coffee.

The pronoun changes with the person; the verb agrees with the thing liked.
cards.englishPhrase: I like coffee.

table.title: gustar — the pronoun changes, not the subject
table.hint: the thing liked is the subject; the pronoun says to whom
table.note: me / te / le / nos / les are indirect object pronouns. The verb agrees with the thing liked, NOT the person.

cards.english: When do you use gusta vs gustan with me?
cards.grammarNote:
The verb agrees with the **thing liked** (the grammatical subject), not the person:

**singular thing** → **me gusta** el café
**plural things** → **me gustan** las galletas

This is the only choice you make — the pronoun stays the same.
cards.englishPhrase: I like cookies.
I like coffee. Do you like tea?
cards.phrase: Me gusta el café. ¿Te gusta el té?

cards.englishPhrase: You like the restaurant near the school.
cards.phrase: Te gusta el restaurante cerca de la escuela.

cards.englishPhrase: We like cookies and chocolate.
cards.phrase: Nos gustan las galletas y el chocolate.

cards.englishPhrase: She likes the food at the café.
cards.phrase: Le gusta la comida del café.

cards.english: How do you clarify or emphasize who likes something with gustar?
cards.word: a él le gusta / a mí me gusta
cards.grammarNote:
**le** and **les** are ambiguous (could be he, she, or you formal). Add **a + person/pronoun** to clarify or emphasize:

**a él le gusta** (HE likes it — not her)
**a mí me gusta** (as for me, I like it — emphasis)

The indirect pronoun (me/le…) is always kept — **a mí** doesn't replace it.
cards.englishPhrase: He likes coffee, but I like tea.
cards.phrase: A él le gusta el café, pero a mí me gusta el té.

contrast.prompt: Why say 'a él le gusta' instead of just 'le gusta'?

b.term: a él le gusta el café

cards.english: How do you say 'I like to cook' — gusta or gustan?
cards.grammarNote:
When the thing liked is an **action** (infinitive), use **gusta** — always singular, even with multiple actions:

**me gusta cocinar** (I like cooking)
**me gusta leer y escribir** (I like reading and writing — still singular!)

An infinitive is treated as one 'thing'.
cards.englishPhrase: I like cooking at home.

table.title: gusta + infinitive (always singular)
table.hint: an infinitive is one 'thing' — always gusta
table.note: Never gustan before an infinitive. Even 'I like cooking and reading' = me gusta cocinar y leer.

cards.englishPhrase: I like to read at home.
You like to cook in the kitchen.
cards.phrase: Te gusta cocinar en la cocina.

cards.english: Name four other verbs that work exactly like gustar.
cards.grammarNote:
Several verbs follow the exact same **pronoun + verb + subject** pattern as gustar:

**encantar** — to love (stronger than gustar)
**interesar** — to interest
**molestar** — to bother / annoy
**doler** — to hurt / ache

All use the same indirect pronouns (me/te/le/nos/les) and agree with the subject.
cards.englishPhrase: I love music. Stress bothers me.
cards.phrase: Me encanta la música. Me molesta el estrés.

table.title: Verbs that work like gustar
table.hint: same pronoun + verb + subject pattern
rows: to love / adore — me encanta el café
to interest — me interesa la música
to bother — me molesta el estrés
to hurt — me duele la cabeza
table.note: All follow singular/plural agreement: me encanta el café / me encantan las galletas.

cards.englishPhrase: I love music. I also love dancing.
cards.phrase: Me encanta la música. También me encanta bailar.

cards.englishPhrase: Her head hurts a lot.
I'm interested in the project at the office.
cards.phrase: Me interesa el proyecto de la oficina.

cards.englishPhrase: Does stress bother you at the office?
cards.phrase: ¿Te molesta el estrés en la oficina?

cards.english: How do you say 'she loves food' and 'my hands hurt'?
cards.word: le encanta la comida / me duelen las manos
cards.grammarNote:
Apply the gustar-family pattern:
**encantar**: le encanta la comida (singular subject → encanta)
**doler**: me duelen las manos (plural subject → duelen)

The verb agrees with the thing, the pronoun marks the person.
cards.englishPhrase: She loves food at the restaurant.
cards.phrase: Le encanta la comida del restaurante.

produce.task: Say 'she loves food' and 'my hands hurt'
produce.answer: le encanta la comida / me duelen las manos
